title: Project Overview & Setup
description: Start with the README to learn what SOUS VIDE is: a Stanford MSL research project that trains drone flight-control policies on visual-inertial data synthesized inside Gaussian-splat scenes. The README lays out the four-part setup path (clone with submodules, build ACADOS, create the 'kitchen' conda environment, download example GSplats), and the environment file pins the exact Python 3.10 / PyTorch + CUDA stack those steps install. The .gitmodules manifest explains a key structural fact for the rest of the tour: the FiGS simulator lives in a separate repository pulled in as a submodule, so simulation code you will see referenced is not in this tree.
languageLesson: Python research projects usually pin their scientific stack with a conda environment file rather than pip alone, because packages like PyTorch+CUDA and nerfstudio need matching native/binary builds. Git submodules keep a heavyweight dependency (here, the FiGS simulator and ACADOS) version-locked but separately maintained.

title: The Simulator Foundation
description: The README points newcomers to the notebooks, and figs_examples is the first one: it builds a Gaussian Splat environment from a phone video capture, then flies an MPC expert through that scene while rendering the onboard camera view. The capture configs supply the OpenCV camera intrinsics for each recording device, and carl.json describes the physical drone (mass, inertia, rotor arrangement) being simulated. Together these three files answer 'where do photorealistic training images come from?' — the question the whole data-synthesis pipeline depends on.
languageLesson: Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) are JSON documents holding ordered cells plus their saved outputs. In research repos they serve as executable entry points and tutorials, while the reusable logic they call lives in an installed package — which is exactly the split you see here between notebooks/ and src/sousvide/.

title: The End-to-End Pipeline
description: sous_vide_examples is the tour's roadmap in executable form: it walks the complete pipeline from generating rollout and observation data, through training the histNet and commNet policy networks, to evaluating the trained policy back in the FiGS simulator from Step 2. Read this notebook as the table of contents for Steps 6-12 — every module the tour visits next is called from somewhere in this file. Seeing the calls in order first makes the individual modules much easier to place.

title: Courses and Method Configs
description: Before any code runs, two families of JSON files declare the experiment. The course files define the flight trajectories as timed keyframes — a looping circuit, a figure-eight infinity, a short production 'button' hop — while the method files define how much data to collect and under what conditions: the data_alpha/beta/gamma progression scales from 3 short rollouts up to 20, and the eval_* family fixes the randomization and sensor-noise regimes used for evaluation (nominal, mocap noise, extreme). These configs are the experimental knobs the paper's results were produced with.
languageLesson: Notice the deliberate naming families (alpha/beta/gamma, nominal/challenged/extreme). Keeping experiment variants as sibling JSON files with identical schemas — rather than as code branches or CLI flags — makes runs reproducible and diffable, a common convention in ML research codebases.

title: Pilots and Network I/O Schemas
description: A 'pilot' is a complete policy described declaratively in JSON. Iceman defines a two-stage architecture, Maverick extends that same histNet/commNet pattern, and Rooster pairs a SIFU history network with a DINO vision feature extractor — the same subnetworks, recombined by configuration rather than by new code. The nnio files define the vocabulary those configs speak: named channels for the basic (scalar), sequence (time-series), and image modalities. Grasp this config-as-architecture idea now, because Step 8's factory exists purely to turn these files into live PyTorch modules.

title: Synthesizing Expert Rollouts
description: This is where training data is born. The rollout generator simulates a VehicleRateMPC expert flying the courses from Step 4 under the randomization the method configs prescribe, recording states, commands, and camera frames. synthesize_helper holds the pure functions behind it (randomized camera-frame sampling and trajectory perturbation), data_compress_helper keeps image stacks affordable by storing them as JPEG bytes, and sousvide_utilities supplies the shared numerical pieces — body-rate frame parameters and relative state/rotation weights — reused later at deployment.
languageLesson: The split between a stateful orchestrator (rollout_generator) and modules of pure helper functions (synthesize_helper, sousvide_utilities) is a deliberate testability pattern: pure functions of arrays can be unit-tested without spinning up a simulator, while the orchestrator owns all I/O and randomness.

title: Rollouts Into Observations
description: Raw rollouts are not yet network inputs. The observation generator replays the recorded flight and image data to assemble exactly the tensors each pilot's declared I/O schema (Step 5) asks for, and the FlightRecorder is the counterpart that captured that state, input, and image data step by step during simulation. This replay-based design means you can re-derive new observation formats for a new architecture without re-flying expensive simulations — the separation that makes the alpha/beta/gamma datasets reusable.

title: Network Foundations and Factory
description: Now the code that consumes Step 5's configs. BaseNet is the abstract PyTorch nn.Module that normalizes the declared input/output configs into concrete tensor shapes, network_helper resolves index and dimension bookkeeping (which channel sits where in a flattened vector), and network_factory reads a pilot's config dict to instantiate or load the right subnetwork. With a fan-in of 8, BaseNet is the single most depended-upon module in the codebase — the contract every architecture in Step 9 must satisfy.
languageLesson: This is the factory pattern in PyTorch form: an abstract nn.Module base fixes the interface (shape normalization, forward signature), and a factory function maps a config string to a concrete subclass. Adding an architecture then means adding a subclass plus a factory case — no changes to training or deployment code.

title: The Network Architectures
description: Five concrete networks all inherit BaseNet's contract and are chosen by config. SVNet is the original command network, pairing a SqueezeNet image backbone with MLP heads; DNNet fuses a small CNN's image features with history and state inputs; Pave adds separate actor and critic heads producing a stochastic policy; SIFU maps flattened dynamics history into a unified feature vector (the 'histNet' role); and feature_extractors wraps large pretrained vision transformers such as ViT-B/16 and DINO. Comparing these is how you see the paper's architectural design space.
languageLesson: These files show transfer learning in PyTorch: pretrained backbones (SqueezeNet, ViT-B/16, DINO) are wrapped as feature extractors and typically frozen, so only the small task heads train. Freezing is done by setting requires_grad = False and/or calling .eval() so batch-norm and dropout layers stop updating.

title: Composing the Pilot
description: Policy is the module that chains the Step 9 subnetworks into the multi-stage pipeline a pilot config describes (for example histNet then commNet), and Pilot wraps that policy in the OODA-style Observe-Retain-Collate-Act loop that a flight controller actually calls each timestep. Pilot ties with BaseNet as the highest-fan-in module in the graph: training, deployment, and data synthesis all talk to a pilot rather than to raw networks, which is why the same object works in simulation and on hardware.

title: Training the Policy
description: With data from Step 7 and a pilot from Step 10, train_policy runs supervised student training: it regenerates observation data on request, then drives the loop over each subnetwork. ObservationData is the PyTorch Dataset wrapping those synthesized tensors for batching, and losses supplies the training objectives plus entropy and load-balance regularizers. This module has the widest reach in the dependency graph, which is why the topology analysis chose it as the natural traversal root through the source tree.
languageLesson: A PyTorch Dataset only has to implement __len__ and __getitem__; DataLoader then provides batching, shuffling, and parallel worker prefetching for free. Keeping per-sample transforms inside __getitem__ is what lets that prefetching overlap with GPU compute.

title: Deployment: Sim to Hardware
description: deploy_figs runs a whole roster of trained pilots closed-loop in the FiGS simulator from Step 2, flight_helper scores each flight on tracking error and inference-time statistics, and command_helper is the hardware-facing layer: RealSense camera setup and capture, plus the state and command coordinate conversions a real drone needs. command_helper has the largest fan-out in the project, reflecting how much plumbing real flight demands — and it is the bridge to the real-world deployment the README flags as coming next.
languageLesson: Note the frame-convention conversions here. Robotics stacks mix conventions (ENU vs NED, body vs world, quaternion orderings), so isolating every conversion in one boundary module — instead of scattering sign flips through the policy code — is what keeps a simulator-trained policy usable on hardware.

title: Visualization and Console UX
description: The visualize package is how researchers actually read their results. plot_3D draws trajectories, waypoints, and quadrotor bodies in 3D (leaning on shared axis-limit and rotor-drawing helpers), plot_time renders state and control time series, plot_synthesize samples and inspects a cohort's synthesized dataset from Step 6, and plot_learning overlays training loss curves with the deployment flight results from Step 12. rich_utilities supplies the progress bars threaded through data generation and training — a high-fan-in module you will have seen imported repeatedly.

title: Packaging and Project Page
description: Two loose ends complete the picture. pyproject.toml is what makes everything above importable: a setuptools src-layout package named sousvide, Python >=3.10, with its scientific and ML dependencies declared — this is why the notebooks can simply 'import sousvide'. The docs directory is the public paper website: a static landing page carrying the abstract and FiGS/SV-Net figures, its Bulma-derived stylesheet, and a small script wiring the navbar, carousels, and video sliders used to present the flight results.
languageLesson: The src/ layout (where = ["src"] in pyproject.toml) puts the package one directory below the repo root so that an accidental local import cannot shadow the installed package. It forces you to test what you actually installed — the reason pip install -e . is part of the setup flow.
